alt: A list of six numbers and a set holding the same values. Checking whether a target is in the list compares it with one cell after another until it matches or the end is reached. Checking the set takes a single step whether or not the target is there.

steps.caption: `nums` holds 6 numbers in order, and `seen = set(nums)` holds the same values. The question is whether 7 is among them.
`7 in nums` compares 7 with `nums[0]`, which is 4. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`7 in nums` compares 7 with `nums[1]`, which is 9. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`7 in nums` compares 7 with `nums[2]`, which is 1. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`nums[3]` is 7, equal to 7. The scan stops with True after 4 comparisons.
`7 in seen` does not scan. The set goes straight to where 7 would be stored and finds it there: True, in one step.
`nums` holds 6 numbers in order, and `seen = set(nums)` holds the same values. The question is whether 5 is among them.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[0]`, which is 4. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[1]`, which is 9. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[2]`, which is 1. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[3]`, which is 7. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[4]`, which is 6. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
`5 in nums` compares 5 with `nums[5]`, which is 2. No match, so it moves to the next cell.
The scan ran off the end after 6 comparisons. 5 is not in `nums`, so the answer is False.
`5 in seen` does not scan either. The set checks where 5 would be stored, finds nothing, and answers False in one step.
`nums` holds 6 numbers in order, and `seen = set(nums)` holds the same values. The question is whether 4 is among them.
`nums[0]` is 4, equal to 4. The scan stops with True after 1 comparison.
`4 in seen` does not scan. The set goes straight to where 4 would be stored and finds it there: True, in one step.
